how-much-to-charge-to-install-sod.html.text:
← Sod installation bid calculator

How much to charge to install sod

Landscapers get shopped on a published $0.55 a square foot installed Facebook special. That number cannot see the grass or the dirt. Two thousand square feet of tall fescue on ready soil you pick up at the farm is a different job from eight thousand square feet of zoysia on clay that needs the existing lawn stripped, hauled off, tilled, graded, and watered three times.

Open the free sod bid calculator

Price pallets, not square feet

Farms sell sod by the pallet. A pallet is commonly 400, 450, or 500 square feet depending on the farm and the cut. You do not buy 4.6 pallets. You buy five. Waste on curves and edges is applied to the lawn first; the leftover coverage on the last pallet is paid for even if it is not laid. That leftover is how a “2,000 foot” special quietly becomes 2,250 feet of farm invoice.

The dirt is usually the job

Ready soil is a site walk. Till-and-grade is a crew morning. Strip-and-haul is dump tickets plus roughly twice the dirt hours of a till. Matching a ready-soil fescue special on a strip-and-haul zoysia lawn is how a sold yard becomes a two-day loss after the first dump ticket.

Fescue, bermuda, and zoysia are not the same install

Fescue is lighter and lays faster. Bermuda sits in the middle. Zoysia costs more at the farm and lays slower because the pads are thicker. The calculator prices the same lawn three ways so you can see which grass still keeps the margin when the homeowner asks you to “just match the other guy.”

Delivery, slope, and watering

Farm pickup is your trailer. Farm delivery is a truckload — leftover pallets still need the truck. Slope slows prep and install, not the drive. Extra watering visits are their own trips; they are not hiding inside the per-foot special.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the sod installation bid calculator. It is not a landscape specification, a soil test, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install sod?

Charge from whole pallets after waste, plus soil prep, delivery, slope, and watering — not a published per-square-foot special. A 2,000 sq ft fescue pickup on ready soil is a different job from 8,000 sq ft of zoysia that needs the existing lawn stripped and hauled off.

How many pallets of sod do I need?

Pallets are sold whole. Multiply lawn square feet by one plus the waste percent, then divide by the farm's pallet coverage (often 400 to 500 sq ft) and round up. Leftover coverage is paid for even if it is not laid.

Why is zoysia more expensive to install than fescue?

Zoysia costs more per square foot at the farm and lays slower because the pads are thicker and heavier. The same lawn in zoysia also often wants more watering visits after install.

Does soil prep change a sod bid?

Yes. Ready soil is a site walk. Till-and-grade is a crew morning. Strip-and-haul adds dump tickets and roughly twice the dirt hours of a till. Those hours do not live in a per-foot special.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is. It is not landscaping, horticultural, irrigation, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. Verify every figure against your own farm tickets and crew times before relying on it.

FOR LANDSCAPERS AND LAWN-INSTALL CREWS

Bid the pallets, the dirt, and the extra work.

Price a sod install the way the trade actually loses money: whole pallets after waste, then soil prep, delivery, slope, and watering — not the published $0.55-a-foot special. You get the job price, what it works out to per square foot and per pallet, and the number below which the lawn loses money.

The lawn

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting hours and farm rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    Why am I paying for 2,250 square feet when the yard is 2,000?

    Because sod is bought by the pallet and pallets do not split. The default 50 × 40 ft lawn is 2,000 sq ft; the 5% waste allowance for cuts and edges brings the requirement to 2,100; and at 450 sq ft per pallet that is 5 pallets, which is 2,250 sq ft paid for and 150 sq ft of leftover. The estimate rounds up because the supplier does. Pricing off the bare 2,000 loses you most of a pallet on every job.

    Why doesn’t the waste allowance just add 5% to the price?

    Because it changes the requirement before rounding, and rounding is what actually costs money. Going from 5% to 10% waste on the defaults takes the requirement from 2,100 to 2,200 sq ft — still 5 pallets, so the price does not move at all. Somewhere past 2,250 it becomes a sixth pallet and the price jumps in one step. Sod cost is a staircase, not a slope.

    Why is labor only $174 on an $1,860 job?

    Because laying sod is fast and the sod is expensive: 6.17 hours at a $28.16 loaded rate against $1,012.50 of sod. It also means the defaults assume the ground is ready. Grading, tilling, killing off existing turf, and hauling away the old lawn are separate prep options, all set to none by default — and on a real re-sod they are usually the larger half of the day.

    Does the price include watering the new lawn in?

    Not by default. Watering visits are an option and start at zero. It is worth pricing deliberately rather than absorbing: new sod needs consistent water for its first two to three weeks, and if you are the one warranting establishment, those visits are your cost. If the homeowner is responsible, say so in writing — sod that dries out in week one is the most common warranty argument in this trade.

vs-a-flat-per-square-foot-special.html.text:
← Sod Installation Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-square-foot special

"$0.55 a square foot installed" is a price for one number, quoted at a lawn whose square footage can look like any other lawn's while everything that actually costs money — the grass, the prep, the pallets, the margin — is different.

What a flat per-square-foot special is

A flat special is the fastest way to quote: one headline rate, read off a yard sign, a Facebook post, or a competitor's postcard and repeated for every lawn afterward. Homeowners shop it because a single number is the easiest thing to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner will ask you to match at a lawn that took the crew a fraction of the time — or several times longer.

The rate behind it was usually set for one lawn — ready soil, common grass, a pickup at the farm — and then reused for every job afterward keyed only to square footage, whether or not the next lawn has an old lawn to strip out, clay to grade, or three watering visits ahead of it.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the lawn's length and width, grass choice, waste allowance, pallet coverage, soil prep, delivery, slope, and watering visits, plus your loaded labor and overhead. It turns that into whole pallets after waste, the dirt-work hours a strip-out or a till-and-grade actually takes, and a walk-away price for this lawn, not a generic one.

What a flat per-square-foot special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges every lawn the same rate per square foot, so a 2,000 sq ft fescue lawn on ready soil and an 8,000 sq ft zoysia lawn that needs stripped, hauled off, and watered three times both get quoted off the same number. Prices the grass, prep, and delivery each lawn actually needs, so this calculator's own numbers for the two jobs above are $0.93 and $1.84 a square foot — about 1.98× apart — even though a flat special would charge both the same rate.
Has no line for stripping out an existing lawn, hauling it off, or the dump ticket that comes with it — a per-square-foot number for "sod install" does not distinguish ready soil from a full strip-out. Prices 19.2 hours of prep labor and an $85 dump ticket for the strip-and-haul job, versus zero for the ready-soil job, because prep hours and dump fees are their own inputs, not folded into one per-foot rate.
Reasons in square feet, but a farm sells whole pallets — so a per-foot special has no way to show a shop it is short a pallet after waste, or paying for coverage it does not need. Orders whole pallets from the area plus waste: 5 pallets (2,250 sq ft bought) for the 2,100 sq ft ready-soil order, 22 pallets (8,800 sq ft bought) for the 8,800 sq ft strip-and-haul order.
Sets a "target margin" by marking cost up a flat percentage — cost × 1.20 for a "20% margin" — which is a markup on cost, not a share of price. Solves for the price that makes margin exactly the stated share of that price. On the 8,000 sq ft zoysia job, a 20% markup on its $11,783.48 cost prices at $14,140.18 and actually clears only 16.7% margin; this calculator's $14,729.35 clears the full 20% the target asked for.
Gives the crew a rate to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a homeowner asks to match a cheaper lawn's price. Reports the walk-away price below which the job loses money — $1,488.28 for the ready-soil job, $11,783.48 for the strip-and-haul job — so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits.

A flat per-square-foot special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied to a lawn whose square footage looks like any other lawn's but whose grass, prep, and pallets are not, and nothing about a yard-sign rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $0.55-a-square-foot special get the price wrong?

Because it charges every lawn the same rate per square foot, and that rate cannot tell a ready-soil job from a strip-and-haul job. This calculator's own numbers for a 2,000 sq ft fescue lawn on ready soil and an 8,000 sq ft zoysia lawn that needs the old lawn stripped, hauled off, and watered three times come out to $0.93 and $1.84 a square foot — about 1.98x apart — even though both are the same kind of job, sod on a lawn.

What does a flat per-square-foot rate leave out?

The dirt work. Stripping out an existing lawn, hauling it off, and the dump ticket that comes with it do not live in a per-square-foot number for "sod install" — that number is usually set from an easy, ready-soil job and then reused for every lawn afterward. This calculator prices 19.2 hours of prep labor and an $85 dump ticket for the strip-and-haul job, versus zero for the ready-soil job, because prep hours and dump fees are their own inputs.

Why do whole pallets matter if the special is priced by the square foot?

Because a farm does not sell a fraction of a pallet, and a per-square-foot rate has no way to show that. This calculator orders whole pallets from the lawn area plus waste: 5 pallets (2,250 sq ft bought) for the 2,100 sq ft ready-soil order, and 22 pallets (8,800 sq ft bought) for the 8,800 sq ft strip-and-haul order, so the bid reflects what the farm actually invoices.

What does solving margin as a share of price get right that a flat number misses?

A flat special, and most rough estimates built the same way, price backward from a markup on cost — add 20% to what the job costs and call that the target margin. That is not the same number: margin is profit divided by price, not profit divided by cost, and a 20% markup on cost actually clears a lower margin than stated. This calculator solves for the price that hits the target margin exactly, so a target set at 20% comes out at 20%, not a smaller number wearing the same label.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local farm prices, labor rates, or what a competitor's coupon charges. It takes the lawn size, grass, waste, pallet coverage, prep, delivery, slope, and watering, plus your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat per-square-foot special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the next lawn stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

vs-aspire.html.text:
← Sod Installation Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Aspire

Two different shapes: Aspire is an account-based business-management platform for running a landscape company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this sod job cost, given its grass, pallets, and prep — before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

Aspire is a cloud business-management platform built for landscape maintenance and construction contractors, irrigation companies, snow and ice management operations, and commercial cleaning businesses, and has been part of ServiceTitan since ServiceTitan's 2021 acquisition of it. It bundles CRM and lead tracking, estimating, scheduling and crew dispatch, purchasing, job costing, mobile crew time tracking, invoicing, and accounting integration into one ongoing subscription account, with plans tiered by a contractor's annual revenue rather than one flat published price — you request a demo to get a quote. Aspire's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity, category, and ownership are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Aspire does. It does not manage a lead list, dispatch a crew across a season, or run payroll. It takes a lawn's length and width, grass choice (fescue, bermuda, or zoysia), a waste allowance, pallet coverage, soil prep, delivery method, slope, and watering visits, plus loaded crew wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the installed price, the pallets ordered after waste, the price per square foot and per pallet, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears your own break-even floor, and a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a signed proposal, an invoice, or a soil or irrigation inspection.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Aspire?

They do different jobs, and a landscape company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually.
